After recovering, he has soup cooked for him, eats a large kettleful, asks his helper Miti' for a large grooved hammer, swallows it, goes to the house of the kamaks, vomits through the vent-hole to fill the interior and force them upward, strikes the Big Kamak with the hammer, kills him, and returns home. In the second story, Eme'mqut lives with his people and is married to Kilu', but they are childless. Eme'mqut goes into the open country, follows a river upstream, and finds numerous luminous, well-dressed people fishing with drag-nets. He falls in love, helps them, and marries a Bumblebee-Woman from among them; these people are Bumblebee people, and his new wife bears many children. Later Kilu' becomes restless, follows the river upstream, finds Eme'mqut among the fishermen, approaches and tramples the Bumblebee-Woman to death, scattering fly-eggs that all become Bumblebees; the fishermen also turn into Bumblebees. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.siberian-koryak-texts-bogoras-archive-l5164-l5311","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/siberian/project-gutenberg/koryak-texts-bogoras.md","passage_locator":{"label":"VOWELS. / I                  E / CONSONANTS. / OPEN    COUNTRY.; lines 5164-5311","start":"5164","end":"5311","translation":"Koryak Texts","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"In this translated portion of a Koryak tale, Big-Kamak swallows a Gull who is revealed as Gull-Woman. Feeling unwell, he lies down, and Gull-Woman uses her woman’s knife from inside his body to rip him open, killing him. She emerges, struggles to reach the cross-pole above his pillow because she is covered with slime, and finally reaches the house-top while his frightened wife lies flat in a corner. Gull-Woman returns home and tells Cormorant-Woman that Big-Kamak swallowed her and she nearly died. Cormorant-Woman decides to be swallowed as well, planning to rip open the devourer with her nails instead of a knife. Cormorant-Woman hides in a cave; Kamak-Woman repeatedly passes by without seeing her until Cormorant-Woman calls out and persuades Kamak-Woman to swallow her without chewing. Kamak-Woman returns home, again complains she is unwell, and asks her husband to cheer her. Cormorant-Woman kills the kamak from inside, tearing old scars with her nails, and emerges, cutting her way through mounds of drifted snow before coming home. A concluding statement says that the kamaks have had enough of these doings, have punished their own bodies, and ceased to walk along the stone. An editorial footnote notes narrative confusion in the roles of Big-Kamak and his wife. The passage ends with the heading and untranslated Koryak text of a new tale titled “Yini'a-fiawgut and Kilu's Marriage with Fish-Man.”","language":"English (with Koryak original)","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Big-Kamak approaches a Gull and swallows her without chewing, then comes home saying he is unwell and lies down to rest.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"While inside Big-Kamak, Gull-Woman uses her woman’s knife to rip open his body from the inside.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Big-Kamak speaks to his wife, asking her to cheer him up; Cormorant-Woman coughs and calls out “Here I am!” but cannot be seen in the dark.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Cormorant-Woman says “Here I am! Swallow me!” Kamak-Woman has difficulty locating her, almost steps over her, then finds her and agrees to swallow her. Cormorant-Woman invites this, and Kamak-Woman swallows her without chewing and goes home.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"After swallowing Cormorant-Woman, Eme'mqut (his son) had no wife. Eme'mqut went out and found outside an old man making ornamented tobacco-mortars, who sent him to an old woman to cook for him, then gave him mortars to haul away without looking back. A reindeer herd and a young woman in a covered sledge appear, and she goes home with him. Later Ila repeats the same sequence with the old man and woman and receives mortars with the same instruction.","summary":"Big-Raven lives with his people, and his son Eme'mqut has no wife. Eme'mqut goes into the open country and meets an old man outside who is making ornamented tobacco-mortars. The old man directs him to enter a house, find an old woman, and have her cook for him. The old woman prepares a meal, takes meat from a kettle, and Eme'mqut eats. The old man then returns home, gives Eme'mqut the mortars, and instructs him to haul them away without looking back at them. Eme'mqut hauls the heavy mortars without stopping or looking back until he sees a large reindeer herd passing ahead; then he stops and looks back and sees a young woman sitting in a covered sledge driving a reindeer-team. He sits in the sledge with her; they drive home together and live there in joy. Later Ila asks how Eme'mqut obtained these things, hears the story of the old man making ornamented mortars, and seeks out the same old man. Ila is told likewise to find the old woman and have her cook. She cooks for him, takes meat from the kettle, and he eats. Raven-Big marries her. His woman Miti’ grows jealous; while Raven-Big is away in the open country, she kills, cooks, and eats the Fish-Woman, saving some meat for her husband. When Raven-Big calls for Fish-Woman, she appears from the rear storeroom carrying cooked food and tells him Miti’ killed and cooked her. The next day Miti’ again attacks and wrings her neck, but when Raven-Big returns the Fish-Woman recovers and again brings food. Later Fish-Woman returns to her home in the sea, warning that Miti’ will eventually kill her; when Raven-Big calls her back she refuses, fearing further violence, and he cannot bring her back. A second tale begins: Kilu and her female relative Yinia-na’wgut go walking; Yinia spots something ahead and tells Kilu to look, and when Kilu comments on it the thing falls down each time. They return home, make a fire, and a Monster-Being arrives and sits on Kilu’s side. Kilu pushes her cousin toward him, saying she saw him first, and the cousin lies down to sleep with the Monster-Being. Kilu escapes out of the house; her clothes are torn off on the trees as she forces her way through, so that she reaches a river naked. The trees tear at her eyes and she bleeds from the nostrils. News spreads, and people wonder about his unusual drum, noting that he has grown old without spirits. Big-Raven keeps his daughter hidden and offers her as a reward to whoever can correctly name the drum’s material. Many neighbors come as suitors and guess various animal skins and living creatures but fail. An evil spirit (kamak) crawls out of the fire, naked except for a cap, and attempts to identify the drum’s material; in the Koryak text he is said to turn into an ordinary woman who assists them. Finally, someone named Miti’ affirms that the drum is made from a small louse and states that they must give their daughter to the kamak. The daughter, seen for the first time and crying, is prepared for a journey to the kamak’s house with three living lines of sledges hauled by whales, reindeer, and white whales, followed by a small cow on which she rides, armed with a large knife and a comb. At the kamak’s house, other kamaks emerge and eat all the reindeer; the girl kills them with her knife until only the original naked kamak and the cow remain. Pursued by him, she throws down her comb, which grows very large; she climbs it, and the kamak cannot follow or eat her. He then prophesies that after she marries a man and bears two children, he will eat her, and he leaves. She later marries a reindeer-breeder, bears two children, and fears the kamak’s return. While her husband is away, the kamak comes and swallows her, but she has concealed a woman’s knife and cuts open his body from within, killing him and emerging alive. The next morning people find a woman working around their house; the mistress asks who she is, and she replies that she is the one who ate them yesterday. Later, when summer comes and it rains, Raven-Man uses the sun as a quid, so that night grows and the land is in complete darkness. In that darkness, people tell a young woman named Can'ai, described as a singer and their daughter, to fetch water because they are thirsty and fear they will die. She goes out groping in the dark, sings that all small rivers are stingy with their water, and then a small bubbling river appears. She fills a Russian iron pail with water and carries it on her back. A man suddenly appears, offers to carry the pail, and follows her home; he identifies himself as River-Man, saying he took pity on the singer. Big-Raven then tells Grass-Woman to give the eater his own offspring. She drops their small son into his mouth, and the eater spits out only broken bones. Big-Raven urges him to eat his own body; the being gnaws the nails of his toes and then consumes his legs, body, arms, shoulders, neck, and throat, finally dying. After some time his remains are burned. Later, Yini'a-na'wgut and her sister sit in darkness after their fire has gone out. They stop up the smoke-hole and say that two figures are coming back, one carrying something on his shoulders; it seems to be Eme'mqut carrying his little son. The pair arrive and ask for fire. The women carry out the fire, feed it with sacrifice, and only then do the newcomers enter. She wakes in the presence of Fish-Man, who has a load of winter-fish, and he marries her. They live together catching many fish and later return to Big-Raven's house, where her family at first insist she became a kamak, but she appears and speaks. A note comments that both kamaks seem to have revived after having been killed and refers to another Koryak text.

In a second episode Kilu envies Yini's Fish-Man husband and arranges to repeat the experience. Both couples live with Fish-Man husbands, are successful in fishing, and the women bear sons.

The household insults her for smelling of excrement, throws the meat to the dogs, and returns her dish empty. Sent with more meat, she is again expelled by Big-Raven and lies in a swoon all day before returning home. She reports that Eme'mqut detained her, praised her as a good girl, and told her to come live with him; she or another woman protests that she has just given birth, but someone promises to carry the newborn wrapped in a coverlet. The Ermine family sets out, but on arriving at Big-Raven's house they are again insulted for their smell and beaten when they try to enter. One person falsely reassures them that the blows are a welcome and urges the mother to enter first; the daughter ironically addresses the old man about this rough 'welcome.' Rejected, the family decides to go live in a cave. They travel to a place rich in edible seaweed, where Ermine-Man falls from a cliff, lies in a swoon, then praises the cliff when he revives. They descend into a cave and sleep there. At night Ermine-Man goes out to urinate, sees upright blocks of ice in the sea, addresses them as the being Stone-Face, and asks about their fishing success. Back inside, he reports that Stone-Face answered that fishing with a drag-net is going well, and a woman says they will now eat cooked fish. A footnote explains that in this region upright rock columns and boulders are regarded as petrified but still living human-like beings; in this story, Ermine-Man only pretends to have seen such a She spends a freezing night near stone-pine bushes. At dawn a herd with iron antlers and a man appear; the man calls to her, and she refuses, saying her real husband has died. He proves that he is Little-Bird-Man and her husband by showing gloves she had made for him. He leads her to a nearby house with reindeer and proposes visiting Big-Raven so people will no longer say she has a bad husband. They arrive at Big-Raven's place with a caravan of pack-sledges. The people announce that Big-Raven's daughter has come with a caravan, though Big-Raven recalls that she departed on foot. She declares that Little-Bird-Man has brought her back. Little-Bird-Man creates many silver driving-sledges, and the couple live together joyfully, traveling in all directions with a caravan. The second story describes Mouse-Girls walking along the seashore. Their mother has the youngest tied on the seashore with diaper strings. The child squeals and repeatedly claims to have found a genuine small nail, which turns out to be only a small shell, so the others strike her. Later she again calls out, describing something with nails, eyes, and whiskers; when they visit her, she has actually found a small ringed seal. A footnote notes another version of this story in Jochelson's \"The Koryak.\"","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Little-Bird-Man and the Mouse-Woman wishes that Big-Raven would delay eating the meat until the next day and decides to use magic. She asks small Mouse-Girl to bring a bundle of magically prepared grass, associated with a shaman’s stick, to Big-Raven’s house and drop it through the vent-hole. He vows not to forgive them and to stun them with blows, asks for his big club, receives it from Miti, and sets out toward the Mouse-Women. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.siberian-koryak-texts-bogoras-archive-l2649-l2830","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/siberian/project-gutenberg/koryak-texts-bogoras.md","passage_locator":{"label":"VOWELS. / I                  E / CONSONANTS. / OPEN    COUNTRY.; lines 2649-2830","start":"2649","end":"2830","translation":"Koryak Texts","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage contains the end of a story about an animate line associated with Big-Raven’s people and a second story, \"Big-Raven and the Kamaks.\" In the first, Frost-Man’s people and people living down the coast try to steal a wakeful line made from a small kamak. While Big-Raven’s people sleep, the down-coast people untie and carry off the line. Big-Raven identifies them as the thieves. Eme'mqut, calling it a \"good line,\" promises to bring it back. He constructs a wooden whale, enters it, travels to the down-coast people, who marvel at the unusual whale and attack it with a harpoon attached to a new line. The small kamak bites into the whale. Eme'mqut quietly tells the kamak he has come to fetch him, then throws berries of Rubus Arcticus into the hunters’ boat. As they eat the berries, he flees home with the new line. After this, Big-Raven’s people keep the line in the inner room so others cannot steal it. The next story begins with Big-Raven deciding to slide down hill. He finds the largest mountain, slides from its summit, and rolls into the porch of the kamaks’ house. Small kamaks call him \"human game\" that has come of its own free will, but he insists he is a man. They take him inside and eat his body joint by joint while he remains alive; they consume him, yet he later comes home because he is a shaman, recovers his senses, and speaks to his wife.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"An animate line complains that Frost-Man’s people wanted to steal it.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"People living down the coast hear about the line, attempt to catch the small kamak and make it into a line, and discuss plans to steal it because it is wakeful.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Big-Raven’s people go to sleep while the line tries and fails to awaken them.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"People living down the coast come, untie the line, carry it away, and thereby steal it.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"After discovering the loss, Big-Raven says that people living down the coast have committed the theft and took the line.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Eme'mqut says that a very good line was taken away and that they will bring it back.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Eme'mqut makes a wooden whale, enters it, travels, and comes to the people living down the coast.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The down-coast people walk around and say that such a whale has never come to them before and that it is a very good whale.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Whale-hunters attack the wooden whale, approach it, and throw a harpoon with a new line at it; the small kamak bites into the whale.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Eme'mqut quietly asks the small kamak why it is biting him and states that he has come to fetch it home.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Eme'mqut throws berries of Rubus Arcticus into the boat of the whale-hunters; they eat the berries while Eme'mqut flees quickly to his house.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Eme'mqut carries away the new line, takes it home, and thereafter the people keep the line in the inner room and stop carrying it out so others cannot steal it.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Big-Raven says he will slide down hill and does so, finding a mountain That is all."","summary":"The passage concludes an episode in which a woman, previously brought from the open country, is revealed to have gone away to give birth secretly outside; the garments or objects she made and hung outside are explained as being all her children together. She is described as a skilful seamstress who had no real reason to live in secrecy. After this, the household lives in joy: Eme'mqut marries Kilu, Ilax marries Yini'a-na'wgut, and when they wish, they travel upstream by river to catch winter fish, then return to their house-mates, kill plenty of game, and lead a happy life, though the narrator does not know what later became of them.

Two short tales of Ermine-People follow. In the first, Ermine-People are living when an Ermine-Man comes home and falsely claims they have been asked to live with Big-Raven's people. They go to Big-Raven's house and try to enter, but Big-Raven's people beat them severely. The Ermine-People withdraw, saying they are rejected, and decide to go live in a cave. They move into the cave, but later are caught by a flood and have to climb upward to escape.

In the second tale, Ermine-People live together, and after some time an Ermine-Woman gives birth to a son. An Ermine-Man announces the birth and asks with what they should cut the navel-string. The Ermine-Man takes the axe home, and only then do they sever the navel-string. In the first episode, a family goes to sleep but is reached by rising sea-water. Initially they accuse each other of having urinated, then realize they are surrounded by water and climb a cliff. Ermine-Woman drags all the children up, though the straps snap. The man climbs first, and one of his sides falls off. Ermine-Woman orders the fallen meat cooked; the man claims a Chukchee left it. They cook and eat the meat. As the kettle water boils the man feels ill and soon dies. The woman then notices that one of his sides is missing and realizes they have unknowingly eaten it. In distress she speaks of going to every cache, even others' caches, and the family turns into real ermines.

The second main episode, "Eme'mqut and the Kamaks," begins with Eme'mqut living with his family and finding a house in the open. A voice from inside greets him as La'wa and asks about his "human game." Eme'mqut replies in character, saying "we two" have killed wild reindeer, and asks about his wife. The speakers say she has just borne a son and add that they, staying at home, have killed a man. They urge "La'wa" to call the spirits and tell him the drum is on the cross-pole. Eme'mqut drums and calls the spirits, putting the kamak-woman and her husband to sleep, then revives the other man and flees with him at night. In the middle of the night the sleeping kamaks get up to urinate, notice their son seems very light of foot and that there are two sets of tracks leading in different directions, but they go back inside and sleep again.

Later their real son La'wa comes home. They greet him as if he had just been there; he insists he has only now arrived and reports an unsuccessful, hunger-filled reindeer hunt. They ask him to call the spirits. He takes the drum, which is described as being made from pieces of skin of women’s breasts sewn together, and calls to the spirits while singing "Trai, Tiroi, trai." The rescued man then lives with Eme'mqut's family, marries a reindeer-breeder's daughter, and they live happily.

In the first, Big-Raven walks along a sand-spit, rejecting several seals and whales by kicking or throwing them back into the sea until he finds a large striped whale that he calls a good catch. After he summons neighboring Chukchee, who rush toward the whale with knives, he becomes frightened, enters the whale’s mouth, drinks its oil until his mouth is full, then jumps out and flies away. A fox sees him and repeatedly asks where he comes from; as he replies \"from the whale\" with his mouth closed and then open, the oil spills onto her back. The fox wrings out her coat in a dogs’ trough to collect the oil, and Big-Raven also gathers oil. The small fox then prepares a berry-and-vegetable cake and sends it to Big-Raven as a payment of gratitude, but the gift kills him, apparently through poison mixed with the berries.\n\nThe second fragment concerns Eme'mqut and Envious-One. Eme'mqut suggests that Envious-One join him in visiting another man and roasting an omasum on a flat stone, then leaves Envious-One and departs after roasting. Later, Eme'mqut marries a fine girl, while Envious-One brings his former wife Little U'wen to his home. After some time the two men agree to compare the beauty of their wives. Envious-One dresses his wife in an overcoat fringed with reindeer mane, repeatedly washes her with liquid from a chamber-vessel and rubs blood into her face while bringing her to the meeting, and feeds her ample whale-blubber. Observers praise her long eyelashes and large buttocks, and Envious-One fusses over her hair, expecting her to win. When Eme'mqut’s concealed wife is finally brought out, however, Envious-One faints at the first sight. He suffers diarrhea from the whale-blubber; after the woman is taken away he recovers, claims he has slept, eats again the matter he had vomited, and faints once more when the woman is brought back.
